title: Digital Ethics, the Law and the Planet
summary: Who owns digital content, how to use and credit it legally, how the law protects personal data and computer systems, what technology costs the planet, and how to weigh up hard ethical choices.
learn: What ethics means in technology, and how to weigh up trade-offs and stakeholders
Copyright, intellectual property and fair dealing, and how to credit sources correctly
Licences: all rights reserved, Creative Commons, public domain and open source
Generative AI and ownership: who owns AI content, and is training on artists' work fair?
The UK GDPR, Data Protection Act 2018 and Computer Misuse Act 1990 in simple terms
The environmental costs of cloud services, AI, e-waste and rare minerals, and greener habits
Using a decision framework to debate a real case (links to TransformED Digital ethics E1, E3, E4 and E6)
intro: Technology brings huge benefits, but every choice has a cost for someone or something. In this topic you will learn who owns digital content and how to use it legally, the laws that protect your data and computer systems, the hidden environmental cost of the cloud and AI, and how to think through hard ethical questions and reach a justified decision.

pages.spec: Explain what ethics means in digital technology and weigh up the benefits and harms (trade-offs) of a technology
pages.summary: Ethics is about right and wrong, which is not always the same as legal and illegal. Every new technology brings benefits and harms, so we ask who it works for, who might be harmed and whether the trade-off is fair.

diagram.title: Smart doorbell camera: the trade-off
diagram.caption: The same gadget looks very different depending on whose point of view you take.

states.label: Benefits
points: The owner sees who is at the door from anywhere
Parcels are less likely to be stolen
Footage can help the police after a crime
Older people feel safer at home

states.label: Harms
points: Neighbours and passers-by are recorded without being asked
Footage is stored on a company's servers
Videos can be shared online to embarrass people
It uses electricity and cloud storage all day, every day

blocks.text: Every time you post a photo, use an AI tool, download a film or buy a new phone, you make choices that affect other people and the planet. This topic is about thinking through those choices carefully.
**[[Ethics]]** means the ideas people use to decide what is **right** and **wrong**. **Digital ethics** applies those ideas to technology: how we make it, how we use it and who it affects.
Legal is not the same as ethical

The **law** is a set of rules made by Parliament that everyone must follow, with punishments if they do not. Ethics is wider. Something can be legal but still unkind or unfair, and laws often lag behind new technology.

head: Legal (the law)
Ethical (right and wrong)
rows: Who decides?
Parliament and the courts
People, communities and society
What happens if you break it?
Fines, prison or being sued
Loss of trust, hurt feelings, harm to others
Example
Copying a whole film and sharing it online is illegal
Posting an embarrassing (but legal) photo of a friend without asking is unkind
Changes how fast?
Slowly: new laws take years
Opinions can change quickly as new technology appears

blocks.text: Trade-offs: benefits and harms

A **[[Trade-off]]** is when you gain something but lose something else. **Technological progress always involves trade-offs.** Cheap, powerful phones connect families across the world, but making them uses rare metals and energy, and they can be addictive.

head: Technology
Benefit
Possible harm
rows: AI chatbots
Instant help with explanations and ideas
Can make up wrong answers; can be used to cheat; uses a lot of energy
Self-service checkouts
Shorter queues in shops
Fewer jobs; harder for some older or disabled customers
Cloud storage
Files available anywhere and backed up
Your data is held by another company; data centres use energy and water
Social media
Keep in touch, share hobbies, local news
Cyberbullying, fake news, time-wasting, data collection
blocks.caption: Every technology has two sides

blocks.text: Who does it work for?

A **[[Stakeholder]]** is anyone affected by a technology: the people who use it, the people who make money from it, and people who never chose to be involved at all. A good question to ask about any design is not just *does it work?* but **who does it work for, and who does it leave out?**

blocks.title: Worked example: homework goes fully online
blocks.context: A secondary school in Fermanagh decides that all homework will be set and handed in online. Who are the stakeholders, and what is the trade-off?
steps: **Teachers:** marking is quicker and nothing gets lost. A benefit.
**Most pupils:** can work on any device and get instant feedback. A benefit.
**Pupils in rural areas with slow or no broadband, or no laptop at home:** they may struggle to complete work. A harm.
**Parents:** can see what has been set, but may need to buy a device. Mixed.
**A fairer version:** keep the online system but open the library computers after school and offer paper copies on request.
blocks.answer: The idea works well for most people but could leave some pupils behind. Spotting who is left out lets you improve the design.

blocks.text: Four quick questions for any technology: **Who benefits? Who could be harmed? Is it fair to everyone? Is it legal?**
A common mistake is to say a technology is simply "good" or "bad". Most are **both**, depending on who uses them, how, and for what. Your answers should weigh up both sides.

The rest of this topic looks at the biggest areas of digital ethics and law: who **owns** digital content, how **personal data** is protected, what counts as **computer misuse**, and the **environmental cost** of our devices, the cloud and AI.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Ethics is about right and wrong; the law is the set of rules everyone must follow.
Something can be legal but still unethical.
A trade-off means gaining something but losing something else.
Stakeholders are everyone affected by a technology, including people who did not choose it.
Always ask who a design works for, and who it leaves out.

check.q: What does **ethics** mean?
o: Ideas people use to decide what is right and wrong
The study of how computers work
check.why: Ethics is about right and wrong; laws are the rules made by Parliament.

check.q: Which statement is true?
o: Something can be legal but still unethical
Ethics and the law are exactly the same
check.why: For example, posting an unkind but legal photo of someone.

check.q: What is a trade-off?
o: Gaining something but losing something else
check.why: Technology usually brings benefits and harms together.

check.q: A neighbour is recorded by your smart doorbell. In this situation the neighbour is a:
check.why: Anyone affected by a technology is a stakeholder, even if they did not choose it.

practice.q: Explain the difference between something being **illegal** and something being **unethical**.
practice.a: Illegal means it breaks the law / a rule made by Parliament with punishments (1); unethical means it is morally wrong / unfair / harmful even if no law is broken (1).

practice.q: Describe **one** benefit and **one** possible harm of AI chatbots.
practice.a: Benefit, e.g. instant help/explanations/ideas (1). Harm, e.g. can give wrong answers / used to cheat / uses lots of energy / privacy of what you type (1).

practice.q: A town council wants to replace its library with an online e-book service. Identify **two** stakeholders and explain how each might be affected.
practice.a: Any two stakeholders (1 each) with a matching effect (1 each), e.g. young readers with tablets: easier access any time; older people without internet: may lose access; library staff: may lose jobs; council: saves money.

pages.spec: Describe intellectual property and copyright: what is protected, for how long, and when fair dealing allows limited use
pages.summary: Intellectual property is a creation of the mind. In the UK, copyright protects original work automatically, usually for the creator's lifetime plus 70 years, under the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988. Fair dealing allows small, fair uses for things like study, review and teaching.

diagram.title: Is it protected?
diagram.caption: Decide whether each thing is protected and how, then click to check.
head: Item
Protected?
How
rows: A song you wrote and recorded on your phone
Yes, automatically
Copyright: no form to fill in
The idea of a game where you build with blocks
No
Ideas are not protected, only the way they are expressed
The C# code for your Year 10 game
Yes, automatically
Copyright protects code as a written work
The Nike tick logo
Yes, registered
Trade mark: a sign that identifies a brand
A new kind of battery invented by a scientist
Only if registered
Patent: protects inventions for up to 20 years
A play by Shakespeare
No, not any more
Copyright ran out long ago: public domain

blocks.text: If you spend a week drawing a comic, writing a song or coding a game, it feels like **yours**. The law agrees. **[[Intellectual property]]** (IP) means creations of the mind: ideas turned into something real, like writing, music, art, inventions, designs and brand names.
Four kinds of intellectual property

head: Type
What it protects
Do you have to apply?
Example
rows: **[[Copyright]]**
Original creative work: writing, music, art, photos, films, recordings and **computer code**
No: it is **automatic** in the UK
A YouTuber's video, a novel, an app's code
**[[Patent]]**
New inventions: how something works
Yes, and it must be granted
A new type of phone hinge
**[[Trade mark]]**
Signs that identify a brand: names, logos, slogans
Yes, to register it
The McDonald's golden arches
Design right
The shape and look of a product
Sometimes (some design rights are automatic)
The shape of a games controller
blocks.caption: Types of intellectual property

blocks.text: Copyright in the UK

In the UK the main law is the **[[Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988]]**. Copyright starts **the moment** an original work is created and recorded in some way (written down, saved, filmed). You do not need to register it or add the © symbol, although the symbol is a useful reminder.

The copyright owner (usually the creator) has the right to decide who can **copy**, **share**, **perform**, **adapt** (change) or **sell** the work. Other people must ask for permission, usually through a **licence** (see the next page).

head: Kind of work
How long copyright lasts (simplified)
rows: Books, songs, art, photos, code
The creator's **lifetime plus 70 years** (counted from the end of the year they die)
Sound recordings
Usually **70 years** from when the recording is released
Films
70 years after the death of the last of the main creators (director, writer, composer)
Ideas, facts, names, short phrases
**Not protected by copyright** (a name or slogan might be a trade mark instead)
blocks.caption: How long copyright lasts in simple terms

blocks.text: Fair dealing: small, fair uses
**[[Fair dealing]]** lets you use a **small part** of a copyright work **without permission** for certain purposes, as long as the use is fair and you **credit** the source. The main ones are:

items: **Private study and non-commercial research**: copying a paragraph into your own revision notes.
**Criticism, review and quotation**: quoting two lines of a song in a review of the album.
**Illustration for instruction**: a teacher showing a short clip of a film in a lesson to teach a point.
**News reporting** (this does not cover photographs).
**Parody, caricature and pastiche**: a funny version of something, as long as it does not take too much.

blocks.title: Worked example: fair dealing or not?
blocks.context: Decide whether each use is likely to be fair dealing.
steps: Ronan copies one diagram from a website into his revision notes and writes the source underneath: **likely fair** (private study, small amount, credited).
Grace quotes one line of a poem in her English essay and names the poet: **likely fair** (quotation, credited).
Callum uploads a whole episode of a TV show to his YouTube channel "for educational purposes": **not fair**. He has copied the whole work and shared it publicly.
A club in Enniskillen prints a famous photographer's picture on T-shirts to sell: **not fair**. It is commercial and uses the whole work without permission.
blocks.answer: Fair dealing is about **small**, **fair** amounts for the right purpose. Copying everything, or making money from someone else's work, is not fair dealing.

blocks.text: **"I found it on Google, so it's free to use"** is one of the most common mistakes. Almost everything online is protected by copyright unless it says otherwise. Being *easy to find* does not mean *free to use*.
**Crediting the creator does not make copying legal on its own.** Naming the artist is good manners, but you still need permission (or fair dealing, or a licence) to use their work.

**Copyright infringement** means using a protected work without permission, for example sharing films or music on illegal streaming sites. The owner can take you to court for money (damages), and copying on a large scale to make money can be a criminal offence.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Intellectual property means creations of the mind.
Copyright is automatic in the UK and covers writing, music, art, films, recordings and code.
Patents protect inventions and trade marks protect brands; both must be applied for.
Most copyright lasts for the creator's lifetime plus 70 years.
Fair dealing allows small, fair, credited uses for study, review, teaching, news and parody.

check.q: In the UK, how do you get copyright for a story you have written?
o: Pay a fee to the government
Add the © symbol, or it is not protected
It is automatic once the work is created and recorded
check.why: Copyright is automatic in the UK.

check.q: Which type of intellectual property protects a company logo?
check.why: Trade marks protect names, logos and slogans that identify a brand.

check.q: For most books, songs and pictures, UK copyright lasts for:
check.why: Lifetime plus 70 years, counted from the end of the year the creator dies.

check.q: Which of these is **most likely** to be fair dealing?
o: Uploading a whole film to share with your class
Selling mugs printed with a famous painting
Copying a full app and changing its name
Quoting two lines of a song in a review, with the songwriter named
check.why: A small, credited quotation for review is a fair dealing purpose.

check.q: Which UK law covers copyright?
o: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
check.why: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 is the main UK copyright law.

practice.q: State **two** types of work that are protected by copyright.
practice.a: Any two: written work/books (1); music (1); art/drawings/photos (1); films/videos (1); sound recordings (1); computer code/software (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between a **patent** and **copyright**.
practice.a: A patent protects an invention / how something works and must be applied for (1); copyright protects original creative work such as writing, music or code and is automatic (1).

practice.q: Saoirse says: "I named the photographer under the picture, so I'm allowed to use it on our band's website." Explain whether she is right.
practice.a: No (1): crediting is good practice but she still needs permission/a licence from the copyright owner (and it is not fair dealing as it promotes the band) (1).

pages.spec: Compare licences for digital content: all rights reserved, Creative Commons, public domain, proprietary and open-source software
pages.summary: A licence is permission to use someone's work, with conditions. 'All rights reserved' is the default; Creative Commons licences let you reuse work if you follow their rules; public domain work is free for anyone; open-source software shares its code.

diagram.title: Match the licence
diagram.caption: Click a licence, then the description that matches it.
pairs: You must ask the owner before using it
Use it for anything, even selling, as long as you credit the creator
Credit the creator and do not use it to make money
Credit the creator and do not change it
Credit the creator and share your new version under the same licence
No copyright: anyone can use it for anything

blocks.text: A **[[Licence]]** is permission from the copyright owner to use their work, usually with **conditions**. When you install an app, stream a song or download an image, you are almost always agreeing to a licence, even if you never read it.
All rights reserved

**[[All rights reserved]]** is the default. If a work does not say anything about a licence, assume the owner keeps all their rights and you must **ask permission** (and maybe pay) before copying or sharing it.
Creative Commons

**[[Creative Commons]]** (CC) is a set of free, ready-made licences that creators can choose so that other people can reuse their work **without having to ask**, as long as they follow the conditions. Each licence is built from four building blocks:

head: Code
Stands for
What you must do
rows: Attribution
**Credit** the creator (every CC licence includes this)
ShareAlike
If you change it, share **your version under the same licence**
NonCommercial
Do **not** use it to make money
NoDerivatives
Do **not** change it: share it only as it is
blocks.caption: The Creative Commons building blocks

blocks.text: These combine into six licences, from the most open (**CC BY**) to the most restrictive (**CC BY-NC-ND**). There is also **CC0**, where the creator gives up their rights so the work is like public domain.
Public domain

Work in the **[[Public domain]]** has no copyright, either because it has **run out** (such as Shakespeare's plays or Beethoven's music) or because the creator **gave it away**. Anyone can use it for anything.
A **recording** or **new edition** of a public domain work can have its own copyright. Beethoven's music is public domain, but an orchestra's 2024 recording of it is not.
Software licences

head: Proprietary software
Open-source software
rows: Can you see the source code?
No: it is kept secret
Yes: anyone can read it
Can you change and share it?
No: you only buy the right to **use** it
Yes, following the licence's rules
Cost
Often paid for, or free with adverts
Usually free
Examples
Microsoft Office, Adobe Photoshop, most console games
Linux, Firefox, LibreOffice, Python

blocks.text: **[[Proprietary software]]** belongs to a company that keeps its code secret; you buy a licence to use it. **[[Open-source software]]** shares its source code so that anyone can study, improve and share it. Some open-source licences (like **MIT**) let you do almost anything; others (like the **GPL**) say that if you share a changed version, your code must be open too, a bit like CC ShareAlike.

blocks.title: Worked example: choosing images for a poster
blocks.context: The Year 10 Digital Technology club is making a poster to **sell tickets** for a games night. They find four images. Which can they use, and how?
steps: Image A, **CC BY**: yes, as long as they credit the creator.
Image B, **CC BY-NC**: **no**, because selling tickets is commercial.
Image C, **public domain** (an old map of Lough Erne whose copyright has expired): yes, no conditions.
Image D, **all rights reserved** photo from a news site: only if they ask and get permission.
Image E, **CC BY-ND**: yes, but they must credit the creator and use it **unchanged**, with no cropping or added text.
blocks.answer: A, C and E can be used (with credit for A and E). B and D cannot, unless the owners give permission.

blocks.text: Most image search engines have a **licence filter** (often under *Tools* or *Usage rights*) that shows only Creative Commons images. Always check the licence on the original page too.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A licence is permission to use a work, with conditions.
All rights reserved is the default: ask first.
Creative Commons: BY = credit, SA = share alike, NC = no money, ND = no changes.
Public domain work has no copyright and is free for anyone.
Open-source software shares its code; proprietary software keeps it secret.

check.q: What does **NC** mean in a Creative Commons licence?
o: NonCommercial: do not use it to make money
check.why: NC stands for NonCommercial.

check.q: Which licence lets you use a photo for anything, including selling, as long as you credit the creator?
check.why: CC BY only requires attribution.

check.q: Shakespeare's plays are in the public domain because:
o: Their copyright ran out long ago
check.why: Copyright lasts lifetime plus 70 years, which ended centuries ago.

check.q: What makes software **open source**?
o: Its source code is available to read, change and share
It has no licence at all
check.why: Open source is about access to the code, not just price.

check.q: A work says nothing about how you may use it. What should you assume?
o: All rights are reserved, so ask first
You can use it if you credit it
check.why: All rights reserved is the default.

practice.q: State what the letters **BY** and **SA** mean in a Creative Commons licence.
practice.a: BY: you must credit/attribute the creator (1). SA: ShareAlike, new versions must be shared under the same licence (1).

practice.q: Explain **one** difference between proprietary and open-source software.
practice.a: Proprietary: source code is secret / you only buy the right to use it (1); open source: source code is available for anyone to read, change and share (1).

practice.q: Explain why an image licensed **CC BY-NC** could not be used on a poster advertising a paid concert.
practice.a: NC means NonCommercial / it cannot be used to make money (1); selling concert tickets is a commercial use (1).

pages.spec: Credit sources correctly with citations and a reference list, and explain how to avoid plagiarism
pages.summary: Plagiarism is passing off someone else's work or words as your own. Avoid it by using your own words, putting quotations in quotation marks, citing sources in your work and listing them in a reference list, and saying when you have used AI.

diagram.title: Anatomy of a website reference
diagram.caption: Click each part of this reference to see what it is for.

rows.label: Wikipedia
rows.detail: Author or organisation. Use the person's surname and initial if there is one; otherwise use the organisation or website name.
Year the page was written or last updated. If there is no date, write (no date).

rows.label: Enniskillen Castle.
rows.detail: The title of the page, in italics if you are typing it.

rows.label: Available at: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enniskillen_Castle
rows.detail: The full web address, so a reader can find exactly the same page.

rows.label: (Accessed: 12 November 2026)
rows.detail: The date you looked at it. Web pages change, so this tells the reader which version you saw.

blocks.text: When you use other people's ideas, words or pictures in your own work, you must say where they came from. This is called **crediting your sources**. It is honest, it lets your teacher check your facts, and it shows how much research you did.

**[[Plagiarism]]** means presenting someone else's work, words or ideas as if they were your own. It includes copying and pasting text, lightly changing a few words of someone else's paragraph, copying a friend's homework, and handing in AI-written work as if you wrote it.
Citations and references

head: Term
What it is
Where it goes
rows: **[[Citation]]**
A short note in your work showing which source an idea or quote came from, e.g. (BBC, 2025)
In the text, right after you use the source
**[[Reference list]]**
The full details of every source you used, in alphabetical order
At the end of your work
Quotation
Someone else's **exact** words, inside "quotation marks"
In the text, with a citation
Paraphrase
Someone else's idea explained in **your own** words
In the text, still with a citation
blocks.caption: Ways of crediting sources

blocks.text: How to write a reference
Schools and universities use different styles. A common one in the UK is the **Harvard** style. For a website it looks like this:

items: **Author or organisation** (Year) *Title of page*. Available at: web address (Accessed: date).

blocks.title: Worked example: referencing a web page
blocks.context: Niamh uses the Wikipedia page about Enniskillen Castle for a history project on 12 November 2026. The page was last updated in 2026 and has no named author.
steps: Author: no person is named, so use the website name: **Wikipedia**.
Title: ***Enniskillen Castle.***
Web address: **Available at: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enniskillen_Castle**
Date accessed: **(Accessed: 12 November 2026)**.
In her writing she adds a short citation after the fact she used: *The castle was built in the 15th century (Wikipedia, 2026).*
blocks.answer: Wikipedia (2026) Enniskillen Castle. Available at: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enniskillen_Castle (Accessed: 12 November 2026).

blocks.text: Crediting images and AI

For a **Creative Commons image**, the Creative Commons organisation suggests **TASL**: **T**itle, **A**uthor, **S**ource (where you found it) and **L**icence, for example: *"Lough Erne at sunset" by J. Smith, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.*

If you use an **AI tool** to help with schoolwork, say so: name the tool, the date and what you used it for. In GCSE coursework, exam boards require you to **acknowledge any AI use**, and passing off AI work as your own counts as malpractice.

blocks.title: Worked example: own words or plagiarism?
blocks.context: The original sentence reads: "Copyright is an automatic right that protects original creative work." Which version is acceptable?
steps: Version 1: *Copyright is an automatic right that protects original creative work.* (no quotation marks, no citation): **plagiarism**.
Version 2: *Copyright is a automatic right which protects original creative works.* (a few words changed, no citation): **still plagiarism**.
Version 3: *You don't have to apply for copyright: as soon as you create something original, it's protected (Intellectual Property Office, 2025).*: **acceptable**: own words plus a citation.
blocks.answer: Version 3 is acceptable: the idea is explained in the pupil's own words and the source is cited.

blocks.text: Swapping a few words for synonyms is **not** paraphrasing. Close the source, explain the idea in your own words, then check it and add a citation.
Keep a list of sources **as you research**: copy the web address and the date into a document straight away. It is much harder to find them again later.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Plagiarism is passing off other people's work or ideas as your own.
A citation is a short note in the text; the reference list gives full details at the end.
Exact words go in quotation marks; paraphrases are in your own words, but both need a citation.
Website reference: Author (Year) Title. Available at: URL (Accessed: date).
Always say when and how you used AI.

check.q: What is plagiarism?
o: Presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own
Quoting a source with a citation
check.why: Plagiarism is passing off others' work as yours.

check.q: Why should a website reference include the date you accessed it?
o: To show how quickly you worked
It is needed for copyright to apply
Web pages can change, so it shows which version you saw
So the website can charge you
check.why: Online content changes over time.

check.q: Where does a reference list go?
o: At the end of your work
At the start of your work
check.why: Full details of sources go at the end.

check.q: Changing a few words in a copied paragraph without a citation is:
check.why: Real paraphrasing uses your own words and still needs a citation.

check.q: What does the **L** in TASL stand for?
check.why: Title, Author, Source, Licence.

practice.q: Explain the difference between a **citation** and a **reference list**.
practice.a: A citation is a short note in the text showing where an idea/quote came from, e.g. (BBC, 2025) (1); a reference list gives full details of all sources at the end of the work (1).

practice.q: Give **two** reasons why you should credit your sources.
practice.a: Any two: it is honest/avoids plagiarism (1); lets the reader check the facts (1); shows your research (1); respects the creator's work (1); may be a condition of the licence (1).

practice.q: Write a Harvard-style reference for this source: the BBC page 'What is copyright?' published 2025, web address https://www.bbc.co.uk/example, which you read on 3 March 2026.
practice.a: BBC (2025) (1) What is copyright? (1) Available at: https://www.bbc.co.uk/example (Accessed: 3 March 2026) (1).

pages.spec: Discuss who owns content made by generative AI and whether training AI on artists' work is fair, considering different viewpoints
pages.summary: Generative AI learns from huge amounts of human-made work, much of it copyrighted. Whether that is fair, and who (if anyone) owns what the AI makes, are open questions that courts and governments are still debating.

diagram.title: AI and copyright: how the debate developed
diagram.caption: Click each event. The story is still being written.

items.label: 1988: computer-generated works
items.detail: The UK's Copyright, Designs and Patents Act includes a rule for works made by a computer with no human author: the person who made the arrangements counts as the author. Few countries have a rule like this.

items.label: 2014: research exception
items.detail: UK law allows text and data mining (computers analysing lots of copyright material) for non-commercial research only.

items.label: Late 2022: generative AI goes mainstream
items.detail: AI image generators and chatbots are used by millions. Artists notice their styles being copied.

items.label: January 2023: Getty Images v Stability AI
items.detail: The photo agency Getty Images starts a court case in London against an AI image company, saying its photos were used for training without permission.

items.label: December 2024: UK consultation
items.detail: The government asks whether AI companies should be allowed to train on copyright work unless creators opt out. Many musicians, writers and artists object strongly.

items.label: November 2025: High Court judgment
items.detail: The court mostly rules against Getty. It decides the AI model did not store copies of the photos, but it did not decide whether training itself is allowed, because the training happened outside the UK.

items.label: March 2026: government report
items.detail: The UK government drops the opt-out plan as its preferred option, says it needs more evidence, and proposes removing the 1988 computer-generated works rule.

blocks.text: **[[Generative AI]]** creates new content, such as text, images, music, voices and video, when you type a prompt. It can produce work so realistic that it is hard to tell from something made by a person. It can be used for good (helping a pupil brainstorm, making a game's background art) or to **mislead**, for example a **[[Deepfake]]** video of a politician saying something they never said.

To learn, an AI model is fed enormous amounts of **[[Training data]]**: billions of web pages, books, photos, drawings and songs, much of it protected by copyright and collected without asking the creators. This raises two big questions that nobody has fully answered yet.
Question 1: Who owns what the AI makes?

head: Possible owner
Argument for
Argument against
rows: The person who typed the prompt
They had the idea and chose the final result
Typing a short prompt is not much creative effort; the AI made the choices
The AI company
It built and trained the tool
Most AI companies' terms say users can use the output; the company did not create this particular work
The artists in the training data
The AI could not work without their art
One output is not usually a copy of any single artist's work
Nobody
Copyright is meant to reward **human** creativity
Then anyone could copy AI work, even if a person put lots of effort into it
blocks.caption: Who should own AI output? (a debated question)

blocks.text: The law differs between countries. In the **USA**, courts and the Copyright Office have said that work made entirely by AI, with no human author, **cannot be copyrighted**, although work where a person adds a lot of their own creativity can be. The **UK** has an unusual 1988 rule for "computer-generated works", but in 2026 the government proposed removing it, while saying that work made by people **with help** from AI should still be protected.
Question 2: Is it fair to train AI on artists' work?

head: Many artists and creators say
Many AI developers say
rows: Permission
Our work was used without asking
The AI learns patterns, like a person studying art; it does not keep copies
Payment
We should be paid, like any other licence
Paying millions of creators would be impossible and slow progress
Jobs
AI copies our style and takes our work
AI is a new tool that creators can use too
Fairness
Companies make money from our work
Strict rules would push AI companies to other countries

blocks.text: Possible compromises include **licensing deals** (AI companies pay to use archives of work), an **opt-out** system (creators can say "don't train on my work"), and **transparency** (AI companies must say what data they used). In the UK the debate is ongoing.

blocks.title: Worked example: the class mascot
blocks.context: Ella types a prompt into an AI image generator to make a mascot for the school robotics team. Then she spends two hours redrawing it by hand, changing the colours and adding the team name. Who could claim to own it, and what should she do?
steps: The **first AI image** involved little human creativity, so in many countries it may not be protected at all.
Ella's **hand-drawn changes** are her own original work, so that part is much more likely to be protected.
She should check the AI tool's **terms** to see what they allow (for example, whether school or commercial use is allowed).
She should **say** the design started with an AI tool, and make sure it does not copy a recognisable character or logo.
blocks.answer: The more real human creativity Ella adds, the stronger her claim. Being open about AI use is the ethical choice.

blocks.text: Do not present **opinions** as facts in this debate. A strong answer says "some people argue... others argue..." and gives a reason for each side before reaching a conclusion.

Making realistic fake images, voices or videos of **real people** without their permission can be hurtful, can be used for bullying or scams, and some kinds are **crimes**. Always label AI-made content honestly.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Generative AI creates realistic text, images, audio and video from prompts.
It is trained on huge amounts of human-made, often copyrighted, work.
Who owns AI output is unclear: the law differs between countries and is changing.
Artists want permission, payment and transparency; AI developers want freedom to train.
Give both sides with reasons before giving your own view.

check.q: What is training data?
o: The huge set of examples an AI learns patterns from
check.why: AI models learn patterns from their training data.

check.q: Why are many artists unhappy about generative AI?
o: Their work was used for training without permission or payment
AI images are always low quality
They are not allowed to use AI
check.why: Permission and payment are the main concerns.

check.q: In the USA, can a picture made entirely by AI with no human author be copyrighted?
o: Only if the prompt is long
No: copyright needs a human author
check.why: US authorities have said purely AI-made work is not protected.

check.q: A deepfake is:
o: A realistic fake image, video or audio made with AI
check.why: Deepfakes can make real people appear to say or do things they never did.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by **training data** for an AI model.
practice.a: The large collection of examples (text/images/audio) (1) that the AI learns patterns from in order to make predictions or generate content (1).

practice.q: Give **one** argument for and **one** argument against allowing AI companies to train on artists' work without paying them.
practice.a: For, e.g. AI learns patterns rather than copying / helps progress / paying everyone is impractical (1). Against, e.g. used without permission / creators lose income or jobs / companies profit from their work (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** ways that generative AI could be used to mislead people.
practice.a: Any two: deepfake videos of real people (1); fake voice calls/scams (1); fake news images (1); AI essays passed off as own work (1); fake reviews (1).

pages.spec: Describe the principles of the UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 and the rights people have over their personal data
pages.summary: Organisations that hold personal data must follow the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018: collect only what they need, use it fairly, keep it accurate and secure, and not keep it too long. You have rights, including to see your data and, in some cases, have it deleted.

diagram.title: Making a subject access request
diagram.caption: Click each step to follow a request to see your own data.

nodes.label: You want to see your data
nodes.detail: For example, what a games company has stored about you.

nodes.label: Ask the organisation
nodes.detail: Email or write to them saying you are making a subject access request. It is usually free.

nodes.label: They check who you are
nodes.detail: They make sure you really are the person the data is about, so they do not give it to the wrong person.

nodes.label: Reply within one month?
nodes.detail: They normally have one month to reply (longer for very complicated requests).

nodes.label: You get a copy
nodes.detail: A copy of your data and an explanation of how it is used and who it is shared with.

nodes.label: Complain to the regulator
nodes.detail: If they ignore you or refuse without good reason, you can complain to the Information Commission.

blocks.text: Your school holds your name, address, date of birth, photo, medical notes and exam results. Your games console knows what you play and when. Your phone knows where you have been. All of this is **[[Personal data]]**: any information that can identify a **living person**, either on its own or combined with other information.

Some personal data is extra sensitive and has stronger protection, such as information about **health**, **religion**, **ethnic background**, **sexuality** and **biometrics** (like fingerprints or face scans).
The law

In the UK, including Northern Ireland, personal data is protected by the **[[UK GDPR]]** (UK General Data Protection Regulation) together with the **[[Data Protection Act 2018]]**. They apply to every organisation that uses personal data: schools, shops, doctors, apps and clubs.

head: Principle (simplified)
In pupil-friendly words
Example of breaking it
rows: Lawful, fair and transparent
Be honest about what you collect and why
An app secretly records your location
Purpose limitation
Only use it for the reason you said
A sports club uses members' emails to sell holidays
Data minimisation
Only collect what you really need
A quiz app asks for your home address
Accuracy
Keep it correct and up to date
A school keeps the wrong emergency phone number
Storage limitation
Do not keep it longer than needed
A shop keeps old customers' card details for 20 years
Integrity and confidentiality (security)
Keep it safe from loss, theft and hackers
Pupil records left on an unencrypted memory stick
Accountability
Be able to prove you follow the rules
No records of who can see the data
blocks.caption: The seven data protection principles

blocks.text: Your rights

head: Right
What it means
rows: Right to be informed
You must be told what data is collected and why (usually in a **privacy notice**).
**Right of access**
You can ask for a copy of the data held about you. This is a **[[Subject access request]]**.
Right to rectification
You can ask for wrong data to be corrected.
**[[Right to erasure]]**
You can ask for data to be deleted in some cases (sometimes called the *right to be forgotten*). It is not automatic: a school must keep some records by law.
Right to object
You can tell an organisation to stop using your data for things like direct marketing.
Right to data portability
You can ask to move your data from one service to another.
blocks.caption: Some of your data protection rights

blocks.text: Who enforces it?

The UK's data protection regulator is the **[[Information Commission]]**. It replaced the **Information Commissioner's Office (ICO)** on **30 September 2026**, under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, with the same job and powers. It gives advice, investigates complaints and can issue fines. For the most serious breaches, fines can reach **£17.5 million or 4% of a company's worldwide yearly turnover**, whichever is higher.

blocks.title: Worked example: the free puzzle app
blocks.context: A free puzzle app for 11 to 14 year olds asks for your full name, date of birth, home address, school and constant access to your location. It shares this with advertising companies but its privacy notice does not mention that. Which principles might it be breaking?
steps: **Data minimisation:** a puzzle game does not need your home address, school or location.
**Lawful, fair and transparent:** it shares data with advertisers without telling you.
**Purpose limitation:** data collected to run a game is being used for advertising.
**What you could do:** refuse the permissions, delete the app, make a subject access request, or tell an adult and report it to the Information Commission.
blocks.answer: At least three principles may be broken. Apps aimed at children are expected to take extra care with their data.

blocks.text: In the UK you must usually be at least **13** to agree on your own to an online service (like social media) using your personal data. Younger children need a parent or carer's consent.
A common mistake is to think data protection law protects **all** data. It covers **personal** data about **living people**. A spreadsheet of football scores or the weather is not personal data.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Personal data is any information that can identify a living person.
The UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 set the rules for using it.
Seven principles: lawful/fair/transparent, purpose, minimisation, accuracy, storage, security, accountability.
You have rights, including access (a subject access request) and, in some cases, erasure.
The Information Commission (formerly the ICO) enforces the law.

check.q: Which of these is personal data?
o: A pupil's name and date of birth
check.why: It identifies a living person.

check.q: A quiz app asks for your home address even though it does not need it. Which principle does this break?
check.why: Only collect what you really need.

check.q: What is a subject access request?
o: Asking to delete a social media account
Asking an organisation for a copy of the data it holds about you
A request to hack a system
check.why: It uses your right of access.

check.q: Who enforces data protection law in the UK from 30 September 2026?
check.why: The Information Commission replaced the ICO.

check.q: A shop keeps old customers' details for 20 years 'just in case'. Which principle is broken?
check.why: Data should not be kept longer than needed.

practice.q: State **two** principles of data protection law.
practice.a: Any two: lawful, fair and transparent (1); purpose limitation (1); data minimisation (1); accuracy (1); storage limitation (1); integrity and confidentiality/security (1); accountability (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** rights that a person has over their personal data.
practice.a: Any two with description: access/see a copy (subject access request) (1); rectification/correct mistakes (1); erasure/deletion in some cases (1); be informed (1); object to marketing (1); data portability (1).

practice.q: A school leaves a list of pupils' medical conditions on a printer in a corridor. Explain which principle has been broken and why it matters.
practice.a: Integrity and confidentiality/security (1); health is extra-sensitive personal data (1); anyone passing could read it, causing embarrassment/harm/loss of trust (1).

pages.spec: Explain in simple terms what the Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes illegal, and identify which law applies in a given situation
pages.summary: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes it illegal to access computers, accounts or data without permission, to do so in order to commit further crimes, to damage or disrupt computers, and to make or supply tools for these crimes.

diagram.title: The Computer Misuse Act offences
diagram.caption: Each layer is more serious than the one above it, with heavier punishments. Click each layer.

items.label: Unauthorised access
items.detail: Getting into a computer, account or files without permission, even just to look. Example: logging in as a friend with a password you saw them type.

items.label: Unauthorised access to commit further crimes
items.detail: Getting in without permission in order to commit another crime, such as fraud or blackmail. Example: getting into someone's account to steal money.

items.label: Unauthorised acts that impair a computer
items.detail: Deliberately damaging, deleting, changing or slowing down a computer or data. Example: spreading malware, or flooding a website so it crashes.

items.label: Acts causing serious damage
items.detail: Attacks that cause, or risk, serious damage to things like hospitals, power, transport or national security. These carry the heaviest sentences.

items.label: Making or supplying tools
items.detail: Making, selling or handing out malware, stolen passwords or hacking tools intended for these crimes.

blocks.text: In the 1980s two men hacked into a British Telecom system and read private messages. When they were taken to court, it turned out there was **no law** that clearly covered hacking. Parliament responded with the **[[Computer Misuse Act 1990]]**, which applies across the UK, including Northern Ireland.
What the Act makes illegal, in simple terms

head: Offence
In simple terms
Example
rows: Unauthorised access to computer material
Getting into a computer, account or files you do not have permission to use.
Guessing a teacher's password to look at the markbook.
Unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences
Getting in **in order to** commit another crime.
Accessing someone's online banking to transfer their money.
Unauthorised acts that impair a computer
Deliberately damaging, deleting, changing or stopping a computer or data from working.
Spreading ransomware, or paying for a "booter" service to knock a game server offline.
Making, supplying or obtaining tools for misuse
Creating, selling or handing out programs or data meant to be used for these crimes.
Selling a keylogger or a list of stolen passwords.
blocks.caption: Main offences under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (as updated)

blocks.text: **Unauthorised access** is the key idea: it means using a computer system in a way you do **not have permission** to. It does not matter whether you damage anything, and it does not matter how easy it was to get in.

blocks.title: Worked example: legal or illegal?
blocks.context: Decide whether each action is likely to break the Computer Misuse Act.
steps: Cian's friend left her laptop logged in, so Cian posts a silly message on her account as a joke: **illegal**. He used her account without permission.
Orla's dad gives her his Netflix password to use on the family TV: **not a Computer Misuse Act offence**. She has his permission (although it may break Netflix's terms).
A Year 10 pupil pays £5 online to flood a rival's game server with traffic so it crashes: **illegal**. This impairs a computer.
A security company is paid by a bank, with **written permission**, to try to break into its systems and report the weak spots: **legal**. This is ethical hacking (penetration testing).
blocks.answer: The difference is always **permission**. With authorisation, testing a system can be a career; without it, it is a crime.

blocks.text: "I was only messing about" and "they left it logged in" are **not defences**. Young people have been arrested and convicted for offences under this Act. The National Crime Agency runs a scheme called **Cyber Choices** to steer young people with computer skills towards legal careers instead.
Which law is it?
At GCSE you will need to know which law fits which situation. Here are the three big ones from this topic:

head: Situation
Law
rows: Copying and sharing a film, song, game or someone's code without permission
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
A company losing, misusing or over-collecting people's personal data
UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018
Hacking into an account, spreading malware or crashing a website
Computer Misuse Act 1990
blocks.caption: Matching the situation to the law

blocks.title: Worked example: one incident, three laws
blocks.context: A hacker breaks into an online music shop, downloads its customer list and the shop's unreleased albums, and posts both online.
steps: Breaking into the shop's system: **Computer Misuse Act 1990** (unauthorised access, with intent to commit further offences).
Posting the unreleased albums online: **Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988** (copying and sharing without permission).

The shop failed to keep customers' personal data secure, so it may also have broken the **UK GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018** (security principle) and must report a serious breach to the Information Commission.
blocks.answer: One event can involve several laws. Even the victim (the shop) can be in trouble if it did not protect personal data properly.

blocks.text: If you are interested in hacking, put those skills to legal use: capture-the-flag (CTF) challenges, the government-backed **CyberFirst** programme and bug bounty schemes let you practise legally.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes unauthorised access to computers illegal.
Getting in to commit further crimes, and damaging or disrupting computers, are more serious offences.
Making or supplying hacking tools or malware is also illegal.
Permission is the key difference between a crime and ethical hacking.
Copyright = CDPA 1988; personal data = UK GDPR/DPA 2018; hacking = CMA 1990.

check.q: Which law makes hacking into someone's account illegal?
check.why: Unauthorised access is covered by the Computer Misuse Act.

check.q: Using a friend's logged-in account to post a message without asking is:
o: Legal because it was already logged in
check.why: You did not have permission.

check.q: What makes ethical hacking (penetration testing) legal?
o: It is done by a teenager
check.why: Authorisation is the key difference.

check.q: Selling malware online breaks the Computer Misuse Act because:
o: It breaks the storage limitation principle
It is a copyright offence only
It is making or supplying tools for computer misuse
check.why: Supplying tools for misuse is an offence.

check.q: A company loses customers' personal data because it was not kept secure. Which law is most relevant?
o: UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018
None: losing data is not illegal
check.why: Keeping personal data secure is a data protection principle.

practice.q: State **two** offences under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
practice.a: Any two: unauthorised access to computer material (1); unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences (1); unauthorised acts that impair a computer/damage data (1); making/supplying tools for misuse (1).

practice.q: Explain why a penetration tester is not breaking the Computer Misuse Act when they break into a company's network.
practice.a: They have permission/authorisation from the owner (1); so it is not unauthorised access, and they report the weaknesses so they can be fixed (1).

practice.q: For each situation, name the law: (a) a pupil shares a pirated game; (b) a pupil guesses a teacher's password; (c) a club posts members' addresses online.
practice.a: (a) Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (1); (b) Computer Misuse Act 1990 (1); (c) UK GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018 (1).

pages.spec: Describe the environmental costs of digital technology, including data centres, the energy and water used by cloud services and AI, e-waste and rare minerals
pages.summary: Digital technology is not weightless. Devices need mined metals and energy to make, the cloud and AI run in data centres that use electricity and water, and old devices become e-waste that should be recycled properly.

diagram.title: The life of a smartphone
diagram.caption: Every stage has an environmental cost. Click each stage.

items.label: Mining raw materials
items.detail: Metals such as lithium, cobalt, copper, gold and rare earth elements are dug from the ground, using energy and water and sometimes damaging land and communities.

items.label: Manufacturing
items.detail: Factories turn the materials into chips, screens and batteries. For many phones and laptops, this stage causes most of their lifetime carbon footprint.

items.label: Transport
items.detail: Parts and finished devices are shipped and flown around the world.

items.label: Use
items.detail: Charging the device, plus the data centres and networks that run your apps, streaming and cloud storage.

items.label: End of life
items.detail: Reuse, repair or recycle it, and the materials can be recovered. Throw it in the bin and it becomes harmful e-waste.

blocks.text: We talk about "the cloud" as if our photos and messages float in the sky. In reality the cloud is millions of computers in huge buildings called **[[Data centre]]s**, and they need a great deal of electricity and cooling.
Data centres: energy and water

A data centre is a building full of **servers** that store data and run websites, apps, games, streaming and AI. They run **24 hours a day**, and the servers get hot, so they need powerful cooling systems.

items: **Energy:** the International Energy Agency (IEA) estimated that data centres used about **415 terawatt-hours (TWh)** of electricity in **2024**, around **1.5%** of all the electricity used in the world. It projected this could roughly **double by 2030**, mostly because of AI.
**Water:** many data centres use water to cool their servers, and more water is used to generate the electricity they need. Some are built in dry areas where water is already scarce.
**Closer to home:** in the Republic of Ireland, data centres used about **22%** of all metered electricity in **2024**, up from about 5% in 2015 (Central Statistics Office figures).

blocks.text: Figures like these are **estimates**, and they change every year as more data centres are built. Always check the source and the year of any statistic you quote.
The cost of AI

**Training** a large AI model means running thousands of powerful computer chips for weeks or months. **Using** AI also takes energy: estimates vary a lot, but generating a long answer, an image or a video usually takes much more computing than a simple web search. Because millions of people use AI every day, the total adds up.

The **[[Carbon footprint]]** of something is the total amount of greenhouse gases (mostly carbon dioxide) released because of it. If a data centre's electricity comes from fossil fuels, its carbon footprint is high; if it comes from wind or solar power, it is much lower. That is why many tech companies are investing in renewable energy.
E-waste and rare minerals

**[[E-waste]]** is thrown-away electrical and electronic equipment: old phones, laptops, chargers, cables, toys and kettles. The UN's **Global E-waste Monitor 2024** reported that the world produced about **62 million tonnes** of e-waste in **2022**, and only about **22%** was properly collected and recycled.

items: E-waste can contain **harmful substances** such as lead and mercury that leak into soil and water if dumped.
It also contains **valuable materials** like gold, copper and cobalt that are wasted if not recovered.
Some e-waste is shipped abroad and broken apart by hand, sometimes by children, in unsafe conditions.

blocks.text: Devices rely on metals such as **lithium** and **cobalt** (for batteries) and **rare earth elements** (for magnets in speakers and motors). Mining them uses lots of energy and water and can damage the environment. Some cobalt has been linked to dangerous working conditions and child labour.

In the UK, the **[[WEEE]]** Regulations (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) aim to stop electrical items going to landfill. A **crossed-out wheelie bin** symbol means *do not put this in your normal bin*. Shops that sell electrical goods must help customers recycle old ones, and council recycling centres, such as those in Fermanagh, accept them for free.

blocks.title: Worked example: why keep your phone longer?
blocks.context: Suppose (as a rough, made-up example) that making a phone causes 60 kg of carbon dioxide, and charging it causes about 2 kg a year. Compare replacing it every 2 years with every 4 years.
steps: Every 2 years: per year = 60 ÷ 2 + 2 = 30 + 2 = **32 kg a year**.
Every 4 years: per year = 60 ÷ 4 + 2 = 15 + 2 = **17 kg a year**.
Keeping the phone twice as long nearly **halves** its yearly footprint, because the big cost was making it.
blocks.answer: Rough estimate only: real figures vary by model. The lesson holds, though: using devices for longer is one of the biggest green choices you can make.

blocks.text: A common mistake is to think the internet and the cloud have **no** environmental impact because you cannot see them. Every stream, upload and AI prompt runs on real hardware somewhere, using real electricity.

blocks.title: Key points
items: The cloud is real buildings (data centres) full of servers that need electricity and cooling.
Data centres used about 1.5% of the world's electricity in 2024 (IEA), and AI is growing this fast.
Data centres can use large amounts of water for cooling.
E-waste is growing and most is not properly recycled; WEEE rules aim to change that.
Mining metals and rare earth elements for devices has environmental and human costs.

check.q: What is a data centre?
o: A building full of servers that store data and run online services
A type of cloud in the sky
check.why: The cloud runs on real data centres.

check.q: Why do data centres often use a lot of water?
o: To make electricity in the building
To water plants on the roof
check.why: Many use water-based cooling.

check.q: What does the crossed-out wheelie bin symbol mean?
o: Do not put this item in your normal bin
The item is made from recycled plastic
check.why: It is the WEEE symbol: recycle it separately.

check.q: For many phones, which stage of their life causes the most carbon emissions?
check.why: Making the device is usually the biggest part.

check.q: What is e-waste?
check.why: Old phones, laptops, chargers and so on.

practice.q: Explain why using cloud storage has an environmental impact.
practice.a: Data is stored on servers in data centres (1) which use electricity 24/7 and need cooling/water, causing carbon emissions (1).

practice.q: Give **two** reasons why e-waste should be recycled rather than thrown in the bin.
practice.a: Any two: contains harmful substances like lead/mercury that pollute soil/water (1); valuable materials like gold/copper can be recovered (1); reduces need for new mining (1); it is the law/WEEE rules (1).

practice.q: Describe **two** environmental costs of training and using AI.
practice.a: Any two: large amounts of electricity (1); carbon emissions if from fossil fuels (1); water used for cooling data centres (1); new hardware/chips need mining and manufacturing (1).

pages.spec: Estimate the energy use of devices and suggest greener digital habits and sustainable design choices
pages.summary: Energy (kWh) = power (watts) × hours ÷ 1000. Rough estimates like this show where small changes make a difference: keeping devices longer, switching off, streaming less and designing efficient software all help.

diagram.title: How much energy does a device use?
diagram.caption: Enter a device's power in watts, how many hours a day you use it, and for how many days. Rough guide (varies a lot by model): phone charger 5 to 20 W, laptop 30 to 60 W, games console 100 to 200 W, gaming PC 300 W or more.

blocks.text: You cannot change how data centres are built, but you **can** change your own habits, and one day you may design the apps and websites other people use. A quick estimate helps you see which changes matter most.
Estimating energy
Electricity use is measured in **[[Kilowatt-hour]]s** (kWh), the same unit on your family's electricity bill. One kWh is the energy used by something with a power of 1,000 watts running for one hour.

items: **Energy (kWh) = power (W) × time (hours) ÷ 1000**

blocks.title: Worked example 1: a games console
blocks.context: A games console uses about 150 W (a rough figure). Seán plays for 3 hours a day. How much energy is that in a year? Assume (for this example only) electricity costs 25p per kWh.
steps: Energy per day = 150 × 3 ÷ 1000 = **0.45 kWh**.
Energy per year = 0.45 × 365 = **164.25 kWh**.
Cost per year = 164.25 × £0.25 = **£41.06** (to the nearest penny).
blocks.answer: About 164 kWh and about £41 a year. This is a rough estimate: real power use and prices change.

blocks.title: Worked example 2: standby
blocks.context: A TV and console left on standby use about 2 W together (rough figure) for the 21 hours a day they are not in use. What is that over a year?
steps: Energy per day = 2 × 21 ÷ 1000 = **0.042 kWh**.
Energy per year = 0.042 × 365 = **15.33 kWh**.
Across 20 million UK homes that would be about 15.33 × 20,000,000 ≈ **307 million kWh**.
blocks.answer: Tiny for one home, but large across a whole country. Rough estimate only.

blocks.text: A common slip is forgetting to **divide by 1000**. Watts × hours gives *watt-hours*; divide by 1000 to get **kilowatt-hours**. Also check you multiplied by the number of **days**.
Greener digital habits

head: Habit
Why it helps
rows: Keep devices longer; repair instead of replacing
Most of a device's footprint comes from making it.
Buy refurbished or pass old devices on
Reuses something that has already been made.
Recycle old electricals properly (WEEE)
Recovers materials and stops pollution.
Switch off rather than standby; turn down screen brightness
Saves electricity every day.
Download favourite songs and shows instead of streaming them again and again
Less data sent from data centres over networks.
Use AI when it genuinely helps, not for things a quick search or your own brain can do
AI requests take more computing than a simple search.
Clear out old files, photos and emails you do not need from cloud storage
Less storage needed in data centres (a small but real saving).
blocks.caption: Greener digital habits

blocks.text: Sustainable design
**[[Sustainable design]]** means designing products to have less impact on the environment over their whole life. Digital designers and programmers can help:

items: **Efficient code:** programs that do the same job with less processing use less energy, especially when run millions of times.
**Lighter websites:** compressed images and fewer auto-playing videos mean less data to send.
**Design for repair:** screws instead of glue and replaceable batteries make devices last longer. Some phone makers, such as Fairphone, build phones with parts users can swap.
**Longer software support:** security updates for many years stop working devices becoming unsafe to use.
**Green hosting:** running services in data centres powered by renewable energy.

blocks.text: Even sustainable choices involve **trade-offs**. A thinner, sealed phone is lighter and more waterproof, but harder to repair. Lower video quality saves data but is less enjoyable to watch. Good designers weigh these up.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Energy (kWh) = power (W) × hours ÷ 1000.
Small savings add up across millions of people.
Keeping, repairing and recycling devices are the biggest green choices.
Stream, store and use AI thoughtfully.
Sustainable design includes efficient code, light websites, repairable devices and green hosting.

check.q: What is the formula for energy in kWh?
check.why: Divide watt-hours by 1000 to get kWh.

check.q: A 50 W laptop is used for 4 hours. How much energy does it use?
Which habit usually saves the **most** carbon over time?
o: Keeping your phone for four years instead of two
check.why: Making a device causes most of its footprint.

check.q: Which is an example of sustainable design?
o: Writing efficient code that uses less processing
Making a website with huge uncompressed images
Gluing a battery in so it cannot be replaced
Ending security updates after one year
check.why: Efficient code uses less energy.

practice.q: A games console uses 120 W and is used for 2 hours a day. Calculate the energy it uses in 30 days. Show your working.
Suggest **three** greener digital habits a pupil could adopt.
practice.a: Any three: keep/repair devices longer (1); buy refurbished (1); recycle properly (1); switch off rather than standby (1); download instead of repeat streaming (1); lower brightness (1); use AI only when needed (1); clear unneeded cloud files (1).

practice.q: Explain **one** way a programmer could make an app more sustainable.
practice.a: e.g. write efficient code (1) so it uses less processing/energy on millions of devices (1); or compress images/data (1) so less data is sent from data centres (1).

pages.spec: Use a structured ethical decision framework to debate a technology case study and justify a conclusion
pages.summary: Hard ethical questions do not have one right answer, but you can reach a good, justified decision by working through the facts, stakeholders, options, harms and benefits, the law, fairness and the environment.

diagram.title: An ethical decision framework
diagram.caption: Work through the steps in order. Click each one for the question to ask.

nodes.label: 1. Facts
nodes.detail: What exactly is being proposed? What do we know, and what do we not know yet?

nodes.label: 2. Stakeholders
nodes.detail: Who is affected? Include people who did not choose to be involved.

nodes.label: 3. Options
nodes.detail: List at least three choices, including doing nothing and a compromise.

nodes.label: 4. Benefits and harms
nodes.detail: For each option, what are the good and bad consequences, and for whom?

nodes.label: 5. Law and rights
nodes.detail: Is it legal (copyright, data protection, Computer Misuse Act)? Does it respect privacy and consent?

nodes.label: 6. Fairness and planet
nodes.detail: Does it work for everyone, including disabled people and those without money or internet? What is the environmental cost?

nodes.label: 7. Decide and justify
nodes.detail: Choose the best option, explain why, and say what would make you change your mind.

blocks.text: Throughout this topic you have met questions with no single right answer. Should AI companies pay artists? Is a doorbell camera fair to neighbours? A **[[Decision framework]]** is a set of steps that helps you think through a hard question carefully, instead of just going with your first feeling.
The seven steps

items: **Facts:** what is actually being proposed?
**Stakeholders:** who is affected?
**Options:** what could we do? Always include a compromise.
**Benefits and harms:** what happens to each stakeholder under each option?
**Law and rights:** is it legal? Does it respect privacy, ownership and consent?
**Fairness and planet:** does it work for everyone? What does it cost the environment?
**Decide and justify:** choose, give reasons, and admit any downsides.

blocks.text: Case study: paying for lunch with your face

A (made-up) secondary school in Northern Ireland wants to install **facial recognition** cameras in the canteen. Pupils would pay for lunch by looking at a camera instead of using a card or PIN. The company says it will speed up the queue.

This is based on real events. In 2021 several schools in Scotland started using facial recognition to take canteen payments. After concerns about children's privacy, they paused it, and the data protection regulator later said the scheme was likely to have broken data protection law.

blocks.title: Worked example: applying the framework
blocks.context: Should the school install facial recognition in the canteen?
steps: **Facts:** cameras scan each pupil's face and match it to a stored face template linked to their lunch account.
**Stakeholders:** pupils, parents, canteen staff, the school, the technology company, and pupils who do not want their face scanned.
**Options:** (A) install it for everyone; (B) do nothing, keep cards and PINs; (C) offer it only to pupils whose parents opt in, with cards still available.
**Benefits and harms:** faster queues and no lost cards, but face scans are **biometric data**, which is extra-sensitive. If it is leaked, you cannot change your face like a password.

**Law and rights:** biometric data has strong protection under the UK GDPR. The school would need a clear lawful reason, a proper risk assessment and, in practice, the freely given consent of parents and pupils, with a real alternative for anyone who says no.
**Fairness and planet:** some systems are less accurate for some skin tones or for twins; extra cameras and servers use energy. Cards already work.
**Decide and justify:** option B or C. A few minutes saved in the queue is not worth the risk to children's most sensitive data, especially when an alternative already works.
blocks.answer: A justified conclusion: do not make it compulsory. If used at all, it must be optional, with consent and a card alternative.

blocks.text: Running a class debate

head: Stage
What happens
rows: Motion
A clear statement, e.g. *This house believes schools should use facial recognition.*
Proposition
The team **for** the motion gives its main arguments with evidence.
Opposition
The team **against** gives its main arguments with evidence.
Rebuttal
Each side answers the other side's strongest point.
Vote and reflect
Everyone votes, then says whether any argument changed their mind.
blocks.caption: A simple debate structure

blocks.text: Useful phrases: *"Some people argue that... because..."*, *"On the other hand..."*, *"The strongest argument is... because..."*, *"On balance, I think... because..."*

In a debate, challenge the **argument**, never the person. And avoid answers that only give one side: the best answers show you understand **why** sensible people disagree before you reach a conclusion.

blocks.title: Key points
items: A decision framework helps you think through hard ethical questions step by step.
Steps: facts, stakeholders, options, benefits and harms, law and rights, fairness and planet, decide and justify.
Always include a compromise option.
Biometric data (like face scans) is extra-sensitive and strongly protected.
A good conclusion gives reasons and admits the downsides.

check.q: Why use a decision framework for an ethical question?
o: It always gives the same answer
It helps you think through the question carefully, step by step
check.why: It structures your thinking so nothing important is missed.

check.q: Which is the best example of a **compromise** option for the canteen case?
o: Make it optional with consent, and keep cards available
Ban all technology from the canteen
check.why: A compromise keeps some benefits while reducing harms.

check.q: Why is a face scan riskier than a PIN if it is leaked?
o: Face scans are not personal data
You cannot change your face like you can change a PIN
check.why: Biometric data is permanent.

check.q: In a debate, what is a rebuttal?
check.why: Rebuttal responds to the other side's points.

practice.q: List **four** steps of an ethical decision framework.
practice.a: Any four (1 each): identify the facts; identify stakeholders; list options; weigh benefits and harms; check law and rights; consider fairness/environment; decide and justify.

practice.q: Give **one** argument for and **one** argument against using facial recognition to pay for school lunches.
practice.a: For, e.g. faster queues / no lost cards or forgotten PINs (1). Against, e.g. biometric data is sensitive/cannot be changed if leaked / privacy / may be inaccurate for some pupils / needs consent (1).

practice.q: A school wants every pupil to use an AI chatbot for homework help. Using the framework, identify **two** stakeholders and **one** legal issue the school should check.
practice.a: Two stakeholders, e.g. pupils, parents, teachers, the AI company, pupils without home internet (1 each); legal issue, e.g. data protection: what personal data pupils type in and where it is stored / age limits / copyright of outputs (1).

glossary.def: The ideas people use to decide what is right and wrong; digital ethics applies them to how technology is made and used.
Gaining something but losing something else; every technology brings both benefits and harms.
Anyone affected by a technology, including people who did not choose to use it.
Creations of the mind, such as writing, music, art, inventions, designs and brand names, that the law can protect.
The automatic legal right of a creator to control copying, sharing, performing, adapting and selling of their original work.
Protection for a new invention that must be applied for; it lasts up to 20 years.
A registered sign, such as a name, logo or slogan, that identifies a brand.
The main UK law covering copyright and other intellectual property.
Using a small, fair part of a copyright work without permission for purposes such as study, review, teaching, news or parody, usually with credit.
Permission from a copyright owner to use their work, usually with conditions.
The default position: the owner keeps all rights, so you must ask permission to use the work.
Free, ready-made licences that let people reuse work if they follow conditions such as BY, SA, NC and ND.
Work with no copyright, because it has expired or been given away; anyone can use it.
Software whose source code is kept secret by its owner; users buy a licence to use it.
Software whose source code is available for anyone to read, change and share under its licence.
Presenting someone else's work, words or ideas as if they were your own.
A short note in your work showing which source an idea or quotation came from.
The full details of every source used, listed at the end of a piece of work.
AI that creates new text, images, audio or video from a prompt.
The large set of examples an AI model learns patterns from.
A realistic but fake image, video or audio clip made with AI, often showing a real person.
Any information that can identify a living person.
The UK General Data Protection Regulation: the main rules on how organisations must handle personal data.
The UK law that works alongside the UK GDPR to protect personal data.
A request to an organisation for a copy of the personal data it holds about you.
The right to ask for your personal data to be deleted in some situations; also called the right to be forgotten.
The UK data protection regulator; it replaced the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) on 30 September 2026.
The UK law that makes unauthorised access to computers, damaging or disrupting them, and supplying hacking tools illegal.
A building full of servers that store data and run online services such as the cloud, streaming and AI.
The total amount of greenhouse gases released because of something, such as making and using a device.
Thrown-away electrical and electronic equipment.
Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment: UK rules that require electrical items to be collected and recycled separately.
A unit of energy (kWh): the energy used by a 1,000 watt device in one hour.
Designing products to have less environmental impact over their whole life.
A set of steps used to think through a hard ethical question and reach a justified decision.
